identity.title: History of prior abdominal surgery (adhesion risk)

technique.how: Ask specifically about any previous abdominal or pelvic operation (open or laparoscopic), prior episodes of bowel obstruction, abdominal radiotherapy, hernias and known intra-abdominal malignancy. Inspect the abdomen for scars, including small laparoscopic port scars, and confirm with the record if the patient is unsure.
technique.prerequisites: None; corroborate from the chart or relatives if the patient cannot give a history.

interpretation.positive_finding: A prior laparotomy makes adhesive small-bowel obstruction the leading cause of obstruction and was the strongest historical predictor of SBO (RR 12.1) in a prospective cohort of acute abdominal pain.
interpretation.negative_finding: A virgin abdomen makes adhesive SBO much less likely, so obstruction in such a patient should prompt a search for hernia, malignancy, volvulus or Crohn disease rather than reassurance.
interpretation.pitfalls: Patients forget or omit laparoscopic, gynaecological and childhood operations; scars may be hidden by skin folds. Prior surgery also raises the likelihood of post-operative abscess or ileus, which the history alone cannot separate from obstruction.
interpretation.changes_what: Prior surgery plus pain/vomiting/distension: raise SBO probability and obtain CT; no prior surgery with obstruction: look for hernia, mass or volvulus and involve surgery early.

sources.citation: Taylor MR, Lalani N. Adult small bowel obstruction. Acad Emerg Med. 2013;20(6):528-544.

Eskelinen M, Ikonen J, Lipponen P. Contributions of history-taking, physical examination, and computer assistance to diagnosis of acute small-bowel obstruction. A prospective study of 1333 patients with acute abdominal pain. Scand J Gastroenterol. 1994;29(8):715-721.

Bohner H, Yang Q, Franke C, Verreet PR, Ohmann C. Simple data from history and physical examination help to exclude bowel obstruction and to avoid radiographic studies in patients with acute abdominal pain. Eur J Surg. 1998;164(10):777-784.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of prior surgery to dismiss obstruction; hernia, malignancy and volvulus cause SBO in the virgin abdomen.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Prior surgery with obstruction plus fever, peritonism or lactate rise suggests strangulation or closed loop: urgent surgical review, do not rely on conservative management.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: History items are reproducible when asked directly; recall of laparoscopic and remote surgery is incomplete.

extraction_notes: Taylor & Lalani 2013 pool sens/spec/LR for history of abdominal surgery, but the paper is not open access and the abstract lists it only as a 'best predictor' without a number, so no pooled estimate could be quoted with location. Bohner 1998 abstract names previous abdominal surgery among the six most sensitive variables without numbers. Only visible number is the Eskelinen 1994 relative risk (12.1), entered with sens/spec/LR null. Owner should transcribe Taylor 2013 history table. Eskelinen 1994 (PMID 7973431, Abstract) reports relative risk 12.1 for previous abdominal surgery; removed from estimates[] because RR is not a schema statistic, so status is not_quantified despite pooled data existing in the unreachable Taylor 2013 tables.
